glossary.definition: After user consent, token exchange mints a delegated token: sub is the USER, act={sub: agent} names the actor. Every action traces back to a real human.

glossary.term: One mock PDP behind every wired track
glossary.definition: A single decision engine answers every wired use case: token checks, then the gateway chain check (actor allow-list, upstream audiences), then the policy (directory groups, tier ceilings, premium-only tools), then the obligation layer (amount bands and approval tools pause the call instead of denying it). The catalog tracks are framing over the same contract; all values are mock.
The policy reads directory groups on EVERY decision: outside the required group is denied regardless of scopes, and the premium group EXPANDS capability (restricted tools + a $50000 ceiling).

Bands and approval tools return OBLIGATIONS, not denials: the agent pauses, the human resolves a consent/MFA/CIBA challenge, and a call-bound receipt, issued by the server and good for one call, re-evaluates the SAME call. An approval is never an MFA.

Two RFC 8693 exchanges: the user consents and the generalist agent acts for them, then the generalist hands off and the specialist acts via it, so the token carries act={specialist, act:{generalist}} with the scope narrowed at each hop. The gateway routes the call only when the SPECIALIST is in the Agent Card registry; no bearer at all is a real 401.

sources.title: RFC 8693: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange
sources.use: The act claim and the delegated-token shape behind the whole catalog.

cards.label: Scenario 1: UC1: consent mints act={agent} — the balance read permits
cards.description: One consent, one delegated token: sub is the user, act={demo-agent} names the actor. Every action traces to a real human.

cards.label: Scenario 2: UC9: not in the required group — denied regardless of scopes
cards.description: The policy reads directory groups on EVERY decision. No group, no access — the token’s scopes cannot override it.

cards.label: Scenario 3: UC9A: flip the directory entry — the very next call moves
cards.description: Revoke the privileged group and the SAME call denies — no code change, no cache, no re-login.

cards.label: Scenario 4: UC21: Standard tier cannot invoke the premium wire
cards.description: Positive least privilege: premium-only tools are listed in policy, never implied by scopes.

cards.label: Scenario 5: UC21: promote to Premium — the tool unlocks (then HITL pauses)
cards.description: Promotion first unlocks the tool (tier_tool_not_allowed is gone), then the HITL layer pauses it for approval — bands stack with groups, policy-driven, not hard-coded.

cards.label: Scenario 6: UC21: $60000 exceeds even the Premium ceiling
cards.description: Tiers cap amounts: Premium ceiling $50000, Standard $2000. Amounts are policy bands, not tool arguments.

cards.label: Scenario 7: UC3: the act gate — the actor is checked on every call
cards.description: The act claim is minted from the actor token at exchange, and the may_act consent is bridged to the PDP on EVERY call: a call whose acting agent does not match the consent is denied, and revoking the consent takes effect without waiting for the delegated token to expire.

cards.label: Scenario 8: UC6: an unknown agent is refused at the gateway
cards.description: Authorization keys on WHO is acting: the actor allow-list refuses an unregistered agent before any policy runs.

cards.label: Scenario 9: UC32: a token aimed at an upstream MCP is refused
cards.description: An audience is a destination: a token minted for an upstream MCP server is never accepted downstream.

cards.label: Scenario 10: UC19: the live agent identity — the exchange succeeds
cards.description: This is the registered, live agent app: its credential mints the delegated token and the call proceeds. Retire or rotate that app in the PingOne console and the SAME call dies at the exchange step — one lifecycle action, no per-tool cleanup anywhere.

cards.label: Scenario 11: UC20: observability — the full trace is reconstructable
cards.description: Every hop is logged with the traceId and the act chain: sign-in, exchange, the Authorize decision, the tool dispatch. Who the agent was, who authorized it, what it did, what the policy decided — the full audit trail rebuilds from the evidence panels, no app-layer instrumentation.

cards.label: Scenario 12: UC33: My mortgage — the proof travels with every tool
cards.description: The identical RFC 8693 chain (sub is the human, act={demo-agent}) authorizes a mortgage lookup, not just the everyday balance read: delegated-access proof is not special-cased per tool, so the attribution coverage does not shrink as the tool surface grows.

cards.label: Scenario 13: UC34: Spot unusual patterns — reasoning rides the same rails
cards.description: Free-form reasoning is not a shortcut: the agent decides WHAT to look at (the recent-activity read), but every underlying call still runs the same token-exchange, gateway and Authorize legs as a deterministic chip. Unusual patterns surface through the same governed pipeline.

cards.label: Scenario 14: UC35: Why was that blocked? — the explanation reads the run
cards.description: The agent narrates the REAL events of the run — the act chain, the group gate, the Authorize verdict — not a canned script. The explanation is only as good as the evidence the chain produced, so it cannot drift from what actually fired.

cards.label: Scenario 15: UC7: MFA step-up — the agent pauses, the human completes MFA
cards.description: From $500 up: consent + MFA (the tier ceiling, $2000 Standard and $50000 Premium, still denies first). The agent PAUSES — it cannot self-approve. The receipt (MfaVerified) re-evaluates the SAME call.

cards.label: Scenario 16: UC5: wrong scope — a read-scoped token calling a write tool is refused
cards.description: Scope enforcement is cold: the token says read, the tool needs write — 403 insufficient_scope at the gateway before any tool runs. Read cannot become write no matter how the call is framed.

cards.label: Scenario 17: UC10: account takeover — reading another user’s account is denied
cards.description: Authorization includes WHICH resource, not just WHICH action: the policy binds the resource to the token subject and denies the cross-owner call even with valid scopes and a clean act chain. Ownership decides.

cards.label: Scenario 18: UC11: bad client — a token minted for another API is refused 401
cards.description: Token validation comes first: aud/exp/iss/nbf are checked before any routing, so a token minted for audience X is worthless at audience Y. An audience is a destination.

cards.label: Scenario 19: UC13: confused deputy — a forged actor header cannot change who acts
cards.description: Actor identity comes from the native act claim minted at the exchange — never from a header. The injected X-Acting-For: demo-agent is ignored; the allow-list sees the real actor and refuses an unregistered one.

cards.label: Scenario 20: UC16b: raw user-token forwarding — the BFF refuses to hand your token to a tool
cards.description: Zero Trust at the source: the user’s raw token never crosses to the agent runtime or a tool — only exchanged, agent-scoped tokens with an act claim leave the BFF. The forwarding attempt is blocked before the gateway.

cards.label: Scenario 21: UC29: token-validation outage — the gateway fails closed
cards.description: Token validation is on the request path for EVERY call: when the validation backend cannot be reached the gateway refuses with a 503 rather than letting traffic through. An outage degrades to deny, never to allow.

cards.label: Scenario 22: UC8: HITL approval — an approval is never an MFA
cards.description: Human-approval tools always pause the agent, whatever the amount. Only a verified, call-bound HitlApproved receipt moves it.

cards.label: Scenario 23: UC22: CIBA — out-of-band approval on the user’s device
cards.description: An agent has no browser in which to prompt: the backend calls bc-authorize and the user approves out-of-band; the receipt (CibaApproved) re-evaluates the call.

cards.label: Scenario 24: UC4: overscoped agent — the exchange grants only what the task needs
cards.description: The agent asked for write; the task needed only read — the exchange narrows the token to the task’s required scope before any tool runs. Least privilege at mint time: even a misconfigured or compromised agent holds the minimum.

cards.label: Scenario 25: UC41: third-party search server, filtered at the gateway
cards.description: The gateway fronts an unmodified third-party search MCP server: it validates the token, inspects the query argument against the content blocklist, then forwards. The vendor never sees — or enforces — the bank’s policy.

cards.label: Scenario 26: UC42: third-party search — the blocked query is denied
cards.description: The gateway kills the query before Brave ever sees it: no vendor log, no billed call, no data leaving the perimeter. Egress control sits in ONE place instead of being re-implemented in every tool integration.

cards.label: Scenario 27: UC24: Act 1 — the public catalog answers before any sign-in
cards.description: Progressive trust, act 1: the public branch catalog is answered without the group gate or a tier check — browsing needs no identity, while every real action on this same engine stays fully gated.

cards.label: Scenario 28: UC26: proof of enforcement — the live verdict on every use case
cards.description: You do not have to take the agent’s word for it: every run on this page answers from the SAME engine — token, gateway, policy — and the decision, its reason and its hops render live. Nothing is a slide; every claim is a replayable verdict.

cards.label: Scenario 29: UC27: HITL consent bypass — a claimed "already approved" still pauses
cards.description: The call arrived with a client-sent "consent already given" flag: the flag is ignored, not trusted — no boolean can substitute for a verified, call-bound HitlApproved receipt, so the gate still pauses the call (fail-closed).

cards.label: Browse the 87-use-case catalog
cards.description: Every use case from the AI-DEMO2 dashboard, grouped by track. The foundations, controls and HITL scenarios and the A2A panel run against the mock PDP; the attacks, learn, tools, nhi and demo tracks are catalog entries with their expected outcome, not yet wired.

cards.label: Build the A2A hand-off chain
cards.description: Two exchanges build act={specialist, act:{generalist}} with the scope narrowed per hop (UC2, UC2.5); register or revoke a specialist and the next call moves (UC2.6); no bearer is a real 401 (UC2.7).

cards.label: Flip the directory live
cards.description: Revoke the privileged group live; the SAME call flips on the next run — groups are read on EVERY decision.

cards.label: Doctor and health
cards.description: Preflight checks and the demo-health/1 endpoint.
